title: Annoyance hunt
summary: A collection of nouns and verbs for hunting the friction and papercuts people meet, from their point of view: confusing copy, extra clicks, slow steps, surprising defaults, noisy output, repeated prompts, dead ends, inconsistent naming and things that work but feel wrong, with friction tours as charters for websites, command lines, videos and docs, every annoyance recorded in the person's own words with how often it happens, how much it hurts, who it affects and how to reproduce it, ranked by frequency times pain and confirmed by a person.
boundaries: Sessions are read-only on live targets with made-up personas and data; booking, submitting or creating runs only on a test target a person named.
Complaints come only from feedback the requester is permitted to share, and keep no personal data; nobody is replied to or contacted.
A person confirms the ranking and every matter of taste; an agent never decides taste.
Workers create nouns and propose verbs; an authorized requester enqueues the proposals worth doing.
Importing the pack writes nothing and enqueues nothing.

nouns.title: A collection of nouns and verbs for hunting the friction and papercuts people meet

value.lets_workers: Hunt the friction people meet, from their point of view: confusing copy, extra clicks, slow steps, surprising defaults, noisy output, repeated prompts, dead ends, inconsistent naming and things that work but feel wrong; walk friction tours as time-boxed charters for websites, command lines, videos and docs; read permitted feedback for complaints in people's own words; count how often each annoyance happens and how much it hurts, rank by frequency times pain, and have a person confirm the ranking; and record each one as a finding with who it affects, how to reproduce it, a fix and a guard.

flow.when: When a surface changes, or complaints pile up.
One charter per session, by an agent or a person.
A different worker or a person debriefs each session.
When the requester can share feedback.
A person who knows the users, before anything is fixed.
Every confirmed annoyance becomes a finding.
When the fix is a matter of taste, options for a person.
The same reproduction and measure on the fixed build, by a different worker.

complements: Charters, sessions and debriefs follow the exploratory testing charters pack; this pack adds friction tours, measures and a ranking.
The usability heuristics review pack judges a design against ten heuristics; this pack counts what people actually hit, and each friction category points at its heuristic.
When reviewers disagree about a pain rating, the persona panel and second opinion pack can take independent views before the person confirms.
Findings, fixes, verification and guards come from the findings to fixes pack; matters of taste go to the taste palettes pack.

nouns.title: How annoyances are hunted, counted, ranked and handed to fixes
nouns.category_reason: A reusable procedure with guardrails, followed by every verb in this pack.

lifecycle: draft-friction-charters writes time-boxed charters from the friction tours, for websites, command lines, videos and docs.
hunt-annoyances walks one charter from the user's point of view, counting actions, waits, prompts and lines, and quoting every hesitation.
collect-complaints reads feedback the requester is permitted to share and keeps each complaint in the person's own words, with no personal data.
rank-annoyances folds duplicates together by fingerprint, counts how often each happens, applies the pain scale and ranks by frequency times pain.
confirm-ranking is a person's verb: someone who knows the users confirms or changes the pain and the ranking.
record-annoyance-findings writes each confirmed annoyance as a finding with its measurement, quote and reproduction, and proposes its fix.
rules: From the user's point of view: count what a person has to do, wait for, read and remember, not what the code does.
Quote the person: an annoyance is recorded in the words of the person or tester who hit it.
Describe the product, never blame the person.
A fix to an annoyance is verified the way it was found: the same reproduction and the same measure on the fixed build, by a different worker.
When the fix is a matter of taste, a person chooses from a palette; an agent never decides taste. The annoyance is still recorded as a finding.
Pain 4, when people gave up, is a design flaw rather than an annoyance; it is recorded as one, with the same evidence.
Made-up personas and test data only on live targets; nothing is booked, bought or sent.
Workers create nouns and propose verbs; they never enqueue.
sources: Charters and sessions follow the exploratory testing charters pack, after session-based test management.
Response-time limits of 0.1, 1 and 10 seconds come from Nielsen's usability engineering work.
The friction categories, scales and rules are written for this pack.

nouns.title: Guardrail: an annoyance starts from what someone said or did
nouns.category_reason: A guardrail is a reusable rule every verb in this work follows, with the check that proves it.

value.rule: An annoyance starts from what a person, or a tester walking a persona's path, said or did, quoted exactly with the step it happened at. A reviewer's opinion of a design is not an annoyance until someone hit it.
value.how_it_is_checked: Every annoyance has a quote naming the session or message, the step and the speaker's role.

nouns.title: Guardrail: describe the product, never blame the person
nouns.category_reason: A guardrail is a reusable rule every verb in this work follows, with the check that proves it.

value.rule: An annoyance describes what the product did, never what the person failed to do: the error appears only after submitting, not the user missed the hint.
value.how_it_is_checked: No annoyance title blames the person; the record checks reject blaming words.

nouns.title: Nine kinds of friction, what each looks like and how to count it
nouns.category_reason: A catalog of friction categories, each with its signals and its measure.

categories.looks_like: Words a person reads twice, asks about or misreads.
categories.measure: Readers who stopped or asked, of all who reached the text.

examples.website: A button that says Submit request where people expect Sign up.
examples.cli: An error naming an internal module.
examples.video: A term on screen the narration never explains.
examples.docs: A step that names a tool before introducing it.

categories.looks_like: More actions than the task needs.
signals: scrolling to find the next step
categories.measure: Actions taken from intent to done, against the shortest path through the same build.

examples.website: Picking the week again after choosing a shift.
examples.cli: A flag needed on every run that could be the default.
examples.video: Pausing to read a card that leaves too soon.
examples.docs: Opening three pages to finish one task.

categories.looks_like: A wait with nothing to show for it.
categories.measure: Seconds from the action to visible feedback; 0.1 s feels instant, 1 s keeps the flow, 10 s loses attention.

examples.website: A confirm button that takes four seconds with no progress shown.
examples.cli: A command that is silent for a minute.
examples.video: A long black lead-in before anything happens.
examples.docs: A search that takes seconds to answer.

categories.looks_like: A default most people change, or one that does something they did not expect.
categories.measure: Share of sessions in which the default was changed or undone.

examples.website: A week picker that opens on last week.
examples.cli: A command that writes to production unless told not to.
examples.docs: An example that uses a setting nobody should copy.

categories.looks_like: Output a person must read past to find what matters.
signals: missing the one line that mattered
categories.measure: Lines printed per run that the person did not need, and repeats of the same line.

examples.website: A banner of notices on every page.
examples.video: Captions that repeat what is on screen.
examples.docs: A page of warnings before the first step.

categories.looks_like: The same question asked twice in one task.
categories.measure: Prompts per task for information already given.

examples.website: A phone number asked for on the form and again at confirmation.
examples.cli: A password prompt for every subcommand.
examples.video: Two sign-up prompts in thirty seconds.
examples.docs: The same setup steps on every page.

categories.looks_like: A state with no way forward except back or starting over.
categories.measure: Sessions that reached the state, of all that reached the step before it.

examples.website: An empty result with no next step.
examples.cli: A command that prints nothing and exits as if it worked.
examples.video: An ending that never says where to go.

categories.looks_like: One thing called two names, or two things called one.
signals: asking whether two words mean the same
categories.measure: Places that use each name for the same thing, across the surfaces people move between.

examples.website: Shift on one page, slot on the next.
examples.cli: session in the command line for the same thing.
examples.video: Narration and screen text that use different words.
examples.docs: A term the product never uses.

categories.looks_like: It works, but people hesitate, distrust it or check twice.
signals: doing it twice to be sure
categories.measure: Sessions with a double check, a repeat or a question about whether it worked.

examples.website: A saved form that reappears with only a faint note.
examples.cli: Success that prints nothing at all.
examples.video: A promise in the title the video never shows.
examples.docs: An example whose output differs slightly from what the page shows.

value.not_an_annoyance: A reaction to looks with no cost to a task, such as disliking a color, is a matter of taste for a palette brief, not a finding.

nouns.title: How much an annoyance hurts, from 1 to 4
nouns.category_reason: A zero-call rule: the same observation always gets the same level.

levels.1: Papercut: noticed it and carried on.
levels.2: Annoying: slowed down or said so.
levels.3: Painful: needed a workaround, help or a second try.
levels.4: Blocking: gave up, or would have without help.

value.who_rates: The person who hit it, or the tester for a persona's path; a person who knows the users confirms or changes it in confirm-ranking, with the reason.

nouns.title: How often an annoyance happens, the score and the rank
nouns.category_reason: A zero-call rule: the same counts always give the same score and rank.

value.share: Occurrences divided by opportunities: the sessions, runs, viewers, readers or messages in which the step was reached.
value.low_confidence: Fewer than three opportunities; the rank stands, and the person confirming it is told.
value.score: frequency level times pain, from 1 to 16.
value.rank: Highest score first; ties go to the annoyance that affects more groups, then the higher pain, then the lower id.
value.severity: A score of 8 or more is P2 and below 8 is P3, as the findings to fixes severity guide places annoyances; a low-confidence entry stays P3 until more sessions confirm it. An annoyance is never P1 or P0: anything that gives wrong results or loses data is an error, and a step people gave up on is a design flaw whose severity triage sets.

nouns.title: Annoyance finding checks, with made-up golden findings
nouns.category_reason: Deterministic checks with made-up known-good and known-bad records; the validator recomputes every verdict.

value.purpose: Deterministic checks every annoyance this pack records passes on top of the findings to fixes record checks: kind annoyance; a measurement naming its friction category, how often it happened against how often it could have, its pain, its score and who it affects; a located quote; steps to reproduce it; a fingerprint naming the category; open when recorded; no blame and no taste reaction; no personal data; and a fix verb and a regression guard proposed. The three good findings are the worked example's; each bad one fails exactly the one check named in fails.

deterministic_checks.why: An annoyance, or a design flaw when people gave up at pain 4, in the findings to fixes pack's terms.
The measurement names one of the nine friction categories.
How often it happened is counted against how often it could have.
How much it hurt is on the pain scale.
The score is written as frequency level times pain; rank-annoyances' acceptance recomputes the product.
The measurement says who it affects.
The quote names where it came from and who said it.
An annoyance comes with the steps that show it again.
The fingerprint names the surface and what goes wrong, not the category, so a person can change the category without splitting duplicates.
A newly recorded annoyance is open.
An annoyance describes the product, never blames the person.
A reaction to looks is a palette brief, not an annoyance.
Quotes and steps hold no email address or phone number.
An annoyance finding holds no personal data, so its sensitivity is none.
Every annoyance carries its proposed fix verb.
Every annoyance carries a guard, such as a page check that counts the steps.

nouns.title: Checklist a person runs before confirming an annoyance ranking

items: Read the top five quotes: did someone really hit each one, in a task that matters?

verbs.title: Draft friction charters from the tours
verbs.summary: Write one to eight time-boxed charters from the friction tours for the target's websites, command lines, videos and docs, each aimed at a named risk such as rising drop-offs or repeated support questions.
verbs.outcome: Charters in the exploratory testing form.

slots.name: target_brief
slots.description: Pin of a brief naming the target, its build, its media and its users.

slots.name: complaints
slots.description: Pins of complaint extracts, if any.

steps: Pick tours for the media the target has, and the risks the brief and any complaints point at.
Write each mission in the explore, with, to discover form, with a made-up persona and what to count.
Time-box each at 45, 90 or 120 minutes and say what is out of scope.

acceptance.check: Every charter validates against template.charter's schema.
Every charter's test ideas name what to count.
Each charter is aimed at a risk the brief or complaints support.

verbs.title: Walk one charter and count its friction
verbs.summary: Walk one friction charter from the user's point of view within its time box, counting actions against the shortest path, waits, repeated prompts and lines printed, and quoting every hesitation at its step.
verbs.outcome: A friction session, with an annoyance proposed for each hesitation.

test_target_named.description: True only when a person named a test target for actions that book, submit or create.

steps: Find the shortest path through the same build first, so every task's actions have something to be counted against.
Walk each task as the persona would; note the time, the step and the exact words at every hesitation, wait over a second or repeated question.
Count lines printed for a command line, and points missed for a video or docs.
Use made-up data only; never book, submit or create anything on a live target unless a person named a test target.
Say what the session did not cover.

acceptance.check: The session validates against template.friction-session's schema.
Every observation has a time, a step and a quote.
Every task has actions taken and the shortest path.

network: Read-only page loads and navigation on the charter's target with made-up data; anything that would book, submit or create runs only on a test target a person named.

verbs.title: Collect complaints from permitted feedback
verbs.summary: Read feedback the requester is permitted to share, such as a support inbox export or survey answers, and keep each complaint in the person's own words with its count, leaving out anything personal.

slots.name: feedback
slots.description: Pins of the permitted feedback exports.

steps: Confirm the requester's permission to read each source; without it, end blocked.
Quote each complaint exactly, trimmed to the complaint itself, and count the messages that make the same one.
Leave out every message that names a person or holds an address, a phone number or an account, and count them with the reason.
Never reply to, forward or follow up on any message.

acceptance.check: The extract validates against template.complaint-extract's schema.
No quote holds a name, address, phone number, email address or account.
messages_read equals the messages with a complaint, plus those excluded, plus those without a complaint.

verbs.title: Rank the annoyances by frequency times pain
verbs.summary: Fold annoyances from sessions and extracts together by fingerprint, count how often each happened against how often it could have, apply the pain scale, and rank by frequency times pain.
steps: Fold together annoyances with the same surface, category and step into one entry, keeping every quote's source.
Count occurrences and opportunities per entry, set the frequency level and flag fewer than three opportunities as low confidence.
Apply the pain scale, score, rank and set the severity by the frequency rule.
Give every entry its reproduction steps and its measure.

acceptance.check: The log validates against template.annoyance-log's schema.
Every level, score, severity and rank recomputes by the frequency rule.
Every observation and complaint in the pinned sessions and extracts is in exactly one entry.

verbs.title: Confirm the ranking (a person)
verbs.summary: A person who knows the users reads the ranked log, confirms or changes pain, category and groups with reasons, marks fixes that are matters of taste, and records the ranking that results. This template performs nothing itself.

slots.name: annoyance_log
slots.description: Pin of the ranked annoyance log.

steps: Read the top entries' quotes and measures, and every low-confidence entry.
Change a rating only with a reason, and mark each fix that is a matter of taste.

acceptance.check: The confirmation validates against template.ranking-confirmation's schema.

verbs.title: Record each confirmed annoyance as a finding
verbs.summary: Write each confirmed annoyance as a findings to fixes finding with its quote, its measurement and its reproduction, and propose its fix, verification and guard; a matter of taste also gets a palette brief, so a person chooses the fix.
verbs.outcome: Annoyance findings, each with its follow-up verbs proposed.

slots.name: annoyance_log
slots.description: Pin of the ranked annoyance log.

slots.name: confirmation
slots.description: Pin of the person's ranking confirmation.

steps: Use the confirmed ranking; leave out entries the person removed and say so.
Give each finding a located quote, a measurement with its category, frequency, pain, score and who it affects, and the reproduction steps.
Propose findings-to-fixes.reproduce, propose-fix, fix, verify-fix and add-regression-guard, and list them in the finding's work as pending; the verification reruns the same steps and measure.
Record every confirmed entry as a finding; for each one the person marked as taste, also write a palette brief instead of choosing a fix.
Record pain 4 as a design flaw; write low confidence into the finding's note and keep its severity at P3 until more sessions confirm it.
Run the findings to fixes record checks and the annoyance checks on every finding.

acceptance.check: Every finding validates against template.finding's schema.
Every finding passes the findings to fixes record checks and the annoyance checks.
Every confirmed entry is exactly one finding, and every taste call also has one palette brief.
